segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the Isha in the original: a portrait drawn in nots, then a poet, an it and a he in one breath. The next verse sounds, at first, like a warning against knowledge itself.

A laptop sticker says stay curious. Somebody once scrawled underneath it: curiosity killed the cat. The Isha's ninth verse sounds like that scrawl. Andham tamah pravishanti ye avidyam upasate: into blind darkness enter those who worship not-knowing. Fair enough. Then: into more darkness, as it were, go those who delight in knowing. So does it really warn people who love learning? Not the way it sounds. Two small words soften it, and two old readings argue about what knowing means here.
screen: `STAY CURIOUS. CURIOSITY KILLED THE CAT.` → `DARKNESS FOR NOT-KNOWING.` → `MORE, AS IT WERE, FOR KNOWING?`

segments.voice: First the small words. Ye means those who. Avidya is vidya, knowing, with that front a meaning not. Then the second line: tato bhuya iva te tamo ya u vidyayam ratah. Tato bhuyah: more than that. And iva: as it were. The text doesn't flatly say knowers go into greater darkness. It says more darkness, as it were. A picture, not a verdict. Ratah: delighting in, as if in knowing alone. Verse ten adds: iti shushruma dhiranam. Iti closes a quotation, like a quote mark. Shushruma: we have heard, from the steady ones who explained it. The Upanishad says, inside its own text, that it's passing on what it heard. Now the two readings, each at its best. Shankara reads avidya here as ritual works, and vidya as knowledge and worship of the gods. Either one, done alone, falls short; the verse warns against one-sidedness inside a life of practice, and real liberation needs something beyond both. Some modern readers, Sri Aurobindo among them, hear vidya as knowing the One and avidya as knowing the many, the world of things. To cling to only one is the darkness; a full life holds both. One reading keeps the verse inside ritual and worship. The other opens it onto the whole world. The text, with its iva, leaves room for both.
screen: `IVA: AS IT WERE.` · `ITI SHUSHRUMA: THUS WE HAVE HEARD.` · `SHANKARA: RITES AND WORSHIP.` · `AUROBINDO: THE ONE AND THE MANY.`

segments.voice: Listen the way a student listens to the steady ones: no notes, no answers, just hearing. Let one sound at a time come and go, near and far, without naming it. If you pray, you can listen inwardly that way too.
Reading the Isha in the original, verses nine and ten: iva, as it were, iti shushruma, thus we have heard, and two readings of what knowing means.
